You're a soldier in one of the bloodiest battles of the war, and you refuse to touch a gun.
It's 1945, Okinawa. You're an army medic, and your faith says you must never kill.
In training, the other men call you a coward. They throw boots at you while you pray. They try to get you kicked out.
Now your unit has to climb a cliff the soldiers call Hacksaw Ridge.
At the top, the Japanese counterattack, and your company runs back down the cliff.
But dozens of wounded men are still up there. So you stay.
Alone, under fire, you drag them one by one to the edge, tie them into a rope, and lower them down.
Every time, you pray. Lord, please help me get one more.
By the time you're done, you've saved about seventy-five men. Some of them, the same men who called you a coward.
Weeks later, a grenade tears into your legs, and a sniper shatters your arm. You still give your stretcher to another wounded man.
In October, President Truman puts the Medal of Honor around your neck. The first ever given to a man who refused to carry a gun.
